summary: Wave-2 cross-family verification of 5 dsv4-wing claims: 4 CONFIRMED (1a, 1b, 2, 3), 1 CONFIRMED with nuance (5), 1 REFUTED-as-quoted with EIA nuance (1c), 1 UNVERIFIED after exhausted recovery attempts (4). One wave-1-derived figure ($19.83/MCF) independently re-derived from EIA's own downloadable series and stands. Multiple additional internal contradictions surfaced during recompute and are reported as findings.
findings: F1 (1a CONFIRMED): average-utility-bills-by-state-2026.md line 22 claims 'national average narrow basket is ~$262/month' while lines 25-27 give its own components: electric $159, gas $60-$120, water&sewer $70-$120. Midpoint sum 159+90+95 = $344 (python-verified). Cartographer's $324 used $80 gas + $85 midpoints (a different split, likely of an earlier revision) - either reconciliation exceeds $262 by $62-$82, so the headline is unsupported by the page's own arithmetic regardless of which sub-midpoints are used. The 17-state table itself averages to $303.47/total column (E 162.82 / G 89.53 / W&S 51.06), corroborating that ~$262 matches nothing on the page.

F2 (1b CONFIRMED): line 62 Hawaii 33.7c/kWh x footnote-specified 900 kWh = $303.30, but the table cell (line 189) says $275* - 9.3% low. The footnote ('Hawaii's electric estimate uses standardized 900 kWh/month') makes the contradiction worse, not better. Row addition itself is fine (275+62+88=425), so the root error is the electric cell. Bonus: the footnote's 'realistic Hawaii electric bill ~$200-$240/month' contradicts its own 515 kWh x 33.7c = $173.56.

F3 (1c REFUTED-as-quoted, with EIA nuance): the phrase '60-70% of natural gas usage = heating' does NOT exist in the current on-disk file or anywhere in content/blog (grep: 0 hits across 4 phrasings; file updated 2026-08-28). The cartographer's supporting figure is a metric conflation: EIA's '43%' (energyexplained/use-of-energy: 'Natural gas, which was used in 58% of homes in 2020, accounted for about 43% of residential sector end-use energy consumption in 2020') is gas's share of residential ENERGY, not heating's share of residential GAS. The page's own cited RECS 2020 tables (CE5.2, ce5.2.pdf fetched from the article's source #4 URL) show gas space heating = 2,886.8 of 4,155.2 T Btu natural-gas end use = 69.47% - i.e., if the author meant 'share of a gas-heated household's gas that goes to heating', a 60-70% range is actually defensible. Both the (missing) page claim and the cartographer's counter-claim need the same treatment: state the metric explicitly.

F4 (1d CONFIRMED): table has exactly 17 state rows (grep -c '<td><strong>' = 17; python: n_rows 17): Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Florida, Georgia, Hawaii, Idaho, Illinois, Massachusetts, Michigan, Mississippi, Montana, New Jersey, New York, Texas, Wyoming - vs title 'Full Comparison (2026)', line 38 'for every U.S. state', line 34 'full state-by-state breakdown'. 33 states missing.

F5 (2 CONFIRMED): what-is-ccf-on-a-water-bill.md line 161 cites USGS Water Basics Glossary as 'conversion reference for cubic feet and gallons.' Fetched the full 138KB glossary (water.usgs.gov/water-basics_glossary.html, 2026-08-29): 'CCF' occurs 0 times, '748' 0 times, 'hundred cubic feet' 0 times; the only cubic-foot entries are flow ('Cubic foot per second'); the only ft3-to-gallon conversion present is for acre-foot (43,560 ft3 / 325,851 gal), not CCF. The tracer's claim stands: the cited glossary contains no CCF-to-gallons conversion.

F6 (3 CONFIRMED): 05-how-to-lower-utility-bills.md line 86 asserts 'EPA: average family saves $70/yr in water + energy[5]' citing epa.gov/watersense/start-saving. The live page (2026-08-29) instead says: 'The average family spends $1,300 per year in water costs, but can save $500 from retrofitting with WaterSense labeled fixtures and ENERGY STAR certified appliances.' Raw-HTML mechanical check: '$70' 0 hits, '70/yr|70 per year' 0 hits, '$1,300' 1 hit, '$500' 1 hit. The companion Showerheads page also carries no $70 (savings there: 2,700 gal/yr, 330 kWh/yr). Prospector's claim fully confirmed.

F7 (5 CONFIRMED, wave-1 arithmetic re-derived): mcf-vs-ccf-vs-therms uses 1 CCF = 1.037 therms, 1 MCF = 10.37 therms (lines 42-44). EIA Natural Gas Monthly Table 'Average price of natural gas sold to residential consumers' (N3010US3, delivered-price series, downloaded 2026-08-29): May 2026 = $19.83 per thousand cubic feet. 19.83 / 10.37 = $1.9122/therm national average. Page's own worked examples: $0.96/therm (FAQ: 50/51.85), $1.01 (scenario C: 157.50/155.55), $1.05 (scenario B), $1.06 (scenario A: 165/155.55) - all 44-50% below the EIA-implied national commodity average. Scenario arithmetic itself is internally correct (re-verified step-by-step); the numbers are merely unrealistic against EIA data, exactly as the wave-1 verifier ruled. Note for fairness: $19.83 includes delivery charges in delivered-to-consumer price; the page frames its examples as supply-only, which softens but does not close the gap (even halved, examples hover at/below the bottom of any defensible range).

F8 (internal cross-checks, new findings for the fix list): (a) line 74 says national average electric bill is '$161' while the quick answer says $159 and the table mean is $162.82; (b) quick-answer water&sewer range $70-$120 vs the page's own water section ('$47/month' national average water + $25-$40 sewer => $72-$87) vs table W&S column mean $51.06 - three mutually inconsistent figures; (c) quick answer says gas $60-$120/75-therm convention but line 100's section uses $1.12/therm => $84 at 75 therms, and table gas mean implies $1.19/therm, while the EIA-derived real delivered price is ~$1.91/therm; (d) one table row fails its own addition (New Jersey 195+130+74=399 vs printed 400); (e) line 291 says Hawaii is '89% higher' than Idaho while the FAQ on line 307 says 'about 48% higher' for the same two numbers. The page is not a candidate for spot-fixes.

F9 (4 UNVERIFIED): how-do-smart-meters-work.md line 190 states 'Exposure is much lower than a typical cell phone.' The article's two listed sources (DOE Grid Modernization; EIA Measuring Electricity) contain zero RF-exposure content (grep: 0 hits in both fetched pages). FCC.gov is bot-walled to this sandbox (403 Access Denied on /engineering-technology/.../radio-frequency-safety, /consumers/guides/5g-and-rf-exposure, and the classic OET FAQ), but the Wayback-archived FCC OET 'RF Safety FAQ' (2003 content, snapshot 20230607) lists 40+ indexed questions - cell phones, SAR, towers, broadcast antennas, pacemakers - and contains NO smart-meter question (grep 'smart meter': 0). Wayback CDX over 1,000 fcc.gov/consumers URLs shows no smart-meter consumer guide. EPA's RadTown RF page now 404s ('Page Not Found | US EPA', fetched 2026-08-29). Conclusion: no authoritative FCC or EPA page making a smart-meter-vs-cell-phone RF comparison could be found; wave-1's 'unverifiable against cited sources' ruling stands, and the sentence carries no usable citation.
